T1A01: One purpose of amateur radio is advancing skills in the technical and communication sides of radio, which is why hams learn and experiment. Providing radio for as many citizens as possible and international contesting are not listed purposes.
T1A02: The FCC (Federal Communications Commission) is the government agency that makes and enforces the rules for amateur radio. The ARRL is a hobby club and helper group, and it cannot enforce the rules.
T1A03: FCC rules say using a phonetic alphabet, like "Kilo Alpha One Bravo Charlie", is encouraged when you identify by voice. It is a helpful tip so others hear your call sign clearly, not a requirement.
T1A04: After you pass, the FCC sends an email with a link so you can download your license grant. That is why you need a working email address on file.
T1A05: Your license is official once it shows up in the FCC's ULS (Universal Licensing System) database. A test certificate or an email from someone else is not the proof.
T1A06: Automatic propagation beacons send signals that let hams hear which bands are open. On 10 meters they are permitted between 28.200 and 28.300 MHz.
T1A07: In FCC rules a space station is an amateur station located more than 50 km (about 31 miles) above Earth's surface. Being in orbit or having people on board does not decide it.
T1A08: A volunteer frequency coordinator, recognized by the local ham community, suggests which channels repeaters should use. This keeps nearby repeaters from interfering with each other. The FCC itself does not pick them.
T1A09: Frequency coordinators are chosen by the amateurs in that local or regional area whose stations are eligible to be repeater or auxiliary stations. It is the hams themselves, not the FCC, who pick them.
T1A10: To be a control operator (the person responsible for a station) at a RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service) station, you also need certification that you are currently enrolled in a civil defense organization. ARRL or ARES membership is not what is required.
T1A11: Willful or malicious interference, meaning deliberately messing up other people's radio signals, is prohibited. International communications on VHF and higher and third-party traffic on digital modes are generally allowed.
T1B01: Technicians can use voice (phone) on 10 meters only from 28.300 to 28.500 MHz. The lower part of the band is for Morse code and digital modes.
T1B02: Any ham with a Technician license or higher can talk to the International Space Station on VHF. You do not need General class or special permission from NASA, though the astronauts have to be on the air.
T1B03: The 6-meter band covers 50 to 54 MHz, so 52.525 MHz fits inside it. The other frequencies belong to other bands, such as 10 meters (28.50 MHz) and 1.25 meters (222.15 MHz).
T1B04: The 2-meter band covers 144 to 148 MHz, so 146.52 MHz is in it. This frequency is a popular national calling frequency for simple radio-to-radio talk.
T1B05: Technicians may use digital modes such as FT8 on parts of 10 meters, 6 meters, and 2 meters. Each of those bands has frequencies where digital is allowed, so all of the choices are correct.
T1B06: On the HF (high frequency, shortwave) bands, Technicians get voice privileges only on 10 meters. The 80, 40, 15, and 30 meter bands do not give Technicians voice operation.
T1B07: The bottom 100 kHz of 6 meters (50.0 to 50.1 MHz) and of 2 meters (144.0 to 144.1 MHz) are for CW (Morse code) only. The other ranges listed do not have that CW-only rule.
T1B08: Where amateur radio is a secondary user, other services such as government or commercial stations may already be using the frequencies. Hams must avoid interfering with them.
T1B09: There are three good reasons to stay off the very edge. Your frequency display might be slightly off, your transmitter can drift, and the sidebands (the signal that spreads out on each side) could spill outside the band. All of these are correct.
T1B10: Above 50 MHz, every amateur band has at least some segment where SSB (single sideband voice) is allowed. It is not limited to repeaters or to higher license classes.
T1B11: On HF, Technicians may use up to 200 watts PEP. PEP, the peak envelope power, is the strongest power in a transmission.
T1B12: Above 30 MHz Technicians can use up to 1500 watts PEP (peak envelope power, the strongest power in a transmission), with a few specific exceptions. You should still use only as much power as you need.
T1C01: The FCC currently issues new licenses in three classes: Technician, General, and Amateur Extra. Novice, Technician Plus, and Advanced are older classes that are no longer issued, though people who hold them can renew.
T1C02: Any licensed amateur can apply for a vanity call sign, which is a call sign you choose yourself if it is available. You do not need a higher class or many years of licensing.
T1C03: International ham communications must be incidental to the purposes of amateur radio, or be remarks of a personal character, like friendly chat. Business talk is not allowed.
T1C04: If the FCC cannot reach you by email, you may face revocation (cancellation) of your station license or suspension of your operator license. That is why you must keep a current email address in your FCC record.
T1C05: A Group D call sign has two letters, a number, and three letters, like KF1XXX. The other formats shown are shorter, and belong to other groups.
T1C06: You may operate from a US-documented vessel in international waters if the ship's master (captain) gives permission. No special FCC permission is needed.
T1C07: You can ask the FCC to renew your license up to 90 days before it expires. Do it within that window so you do not lose your privileges.
T1C08: An amateur license lasts ten years, and you can renew it for another ten.
T1C09: If your license expires, you have a two-year grace period in which you can still renew it. After that, you must take the exam again.
T1C10: You may transmit once your license grant shows up in the FCC license database. A test certificate, a posting on the ARRL (the national ham radio association) website, or a paper copy in the mail does not count.
T1C11: During the grace period you may not transmit. You must wait until the renewal is finished, so renew before your license expires and avoid the pause.
T1D01: FCC-licensed hams may not talk with a country whose government has told the ITU (International Telecommunication Union, the world radio organization) that it objects to such communications. The ARRL and IARU cannot ban countries.
T1D02: Broadcasting, meaning sending signals meant for the general public, is prohibited. Event announcements, Morse code practice, and telemetry (sending measurements) or remote-control commands are allowed one-way transmissions.
T1D03: Messages with hidden meaning, called codes or ciphers, are generally banned. The exception is control commands sent to space stations or model craft, where it keeps others from taking over the control signal.
T1D04: Music is generally not allowed on amateur radio. The exception is when it is incidental (accidentally in the background) during an authorized retransmission of communications with a manned spacecraft.
T1D05: You may announce equipment for sale or trade if it is not done on a regular basis. Doing it often would make the station a business, which is not allowed.
T1D06: Indecent or obscene language is simply prohibited on amateur frequencies. There is no word list, because any language of that kind is not allowed.
T1D07: An auxiliary station sends one-way transmissions linking things like a remote repeater receiver to the main repeater transmitter. It is a helper link, not a backup radio.
T1D08: A control operator can be paid when the communication is part of classroom instruction at an educational institution, such as a teacher running a radio class. The other examples are not allowed.
T1D09: Amateur stations may help with broadcasting or news gathering only when no other means is available and the communication is directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property.
T1D10: The FCC defines broadcasting as transmissions meant to be received by the general public. Two-way chats and messages for other amateurs are not broadcasting.
T1D11: You do not have to identify when sending signals to control model craft, such as a model plane or boat. Short adjustments and low power do not excuse you from identifying.
T1D12: Test transmissions must include station identification with your call sign. There is no required time of day and no need to notify the FCC.
T1E01: A station may never transmit without a control operator, which is the licensed person responsible for it. Even a repeater running automatically has a control operator.
T1E02: Any amateur who is allowed to transmit on the satellite uplink frequency can be the control operator. No special satellite certificate, class, or AMSAT membership is needed.
T1E03: The station licensee, the person whose license covers the station, chooses who the control operator is. Other licensed operators or the FCC do not make that choice.
T1E04: Your frequency privileges depend on the license class of the control operator, the person running the station at that moment. The rights printed on the grant or the highest class nearby do not decide this.
T1E05: The control point is the place where the control operator performs the control function. It does not have to be where the antenna or the radio is.
T1E06: A Technician licensee may never be control operator on frequencies set aside for Amateur Extra, except in emergencies. Another operator's designation or a club trustee's higher license does not change your privileges.
T1E07: When someone else is the control operator, both that control operator and the station licensee share responsibility for proper operation of the station.
T1E08: A repeater is the classic example of automatic control, meaning it runs by itself while its control operator is not at the control point (the place where the station is controlled). Controlling a station over the internet is remote control instead.
T1E09: Any amateur station can be remotely controlled, meaning operated from somewhere else. Repeaters are not the only stations that can be.
T1E10: Remote control means operating a station from a distance, such as over the internet. Controlling model craft is a different kind of operation, and an SDR is simply a type of radio.
T1E11: A control operator is a licensed amateur chosen by the station licensee to be responsible for the station's transmissions and for following FCC rules. The licensee and the person speaking may be different people.
T1F01: You must make your station and its records available to an FCC representative at any time they request it. There is no waiting period and no warrant needed.
T1F02: Even when using a tactical call sign like "Race Headquarters", you must give your FCC-assigned call sign at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at its end. The tactical name does not replace it.
T1F03: You must say your call sign at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of it. Think of it as a regular name tag check.
T1F04: When you identify by voice, you must use English. Other languages cannot be used for identification.
T1F05: If you transmit by voice, you may identify using either voice (phone) or CW (Morse code). You do not have to add an extra ending signal like R or RPT.
T1F06: With phone you may use words like stroke, slant, or slash to say the "/" mark in a self-assigned indicator, so all of the choices are correct. For example, "KL7CC stroke W3" tells people where you are operating.
T1F07: A person who is not licensed can speak through your station to a foreign station only if that country has a third-party agreement with the US. The person need not be a citizen.
T1F08: Third-party communications are messages passed from one amateur control operator to another on behalf of a third person. It does not mean three stations talking.
T1F09: A repeater station receives a signal and retransmits it at the same time on a different channel. This lets hand-held radios talk over longer distances.
T1F10: If a repeater accidentally retransmits a signal that breaks the rules, the control operator of the station that sent the original signal is the one accountable. The repeater is just passing it along.
T1F11: To get a club station license grant the club must have at least four members. The trustee does not need an Extra Class license, and registering with the ARRL is not required.
T2A01: A repeater listens on one frequency and transmits on another, and on 2 meters the usual gap between them is 600 kHz (kilohertz, a unit of frequency). Your radio can add or subtract that gap for you.
T2A02: 146.520 MHz (megahertz) is the national calling frequency for FM simplex on 2 meters. Think of it as a meeting spot where hams call each other directly and then move to another frequency to chat.
T2A03: On the 70-centimeter band the usual repeater offset is 5 MHz (megahertz, a unit of frequency). That is larger than the 600 kHz used on 2 meters, so do not mix the two up.
T2A04: On a repeater you simply say the other station's call sign and then your own, like saying "Hi Sam, this is Alex." No special prefix like "CQ" is needed, since you already know who you want to reach.
T2A05: When you hear someone call CQ (a general call meaning anyone may answer), you reply with their call sign first and then yours. That way they know right away you are answering them.
T2A06: To find someone to talk to when not using a repeater, call "CQ" a few times, say "this is" and your call sign, then stop and listen. CQ means you are calling any station, and pausing lets people reply.
T2A07: A repeater listens on one frequency and transmits on another. The repeater offset is the difference between those two frequencies.
T2A08: CQ is a general call that means "calling any station," like shouting "Is anybody out there?" Any ham who hears it may answer.
T2A09: On a repeater, saying your call sign followed by "listening" tells others you are around and happy to chat. "CQ" is more common on open frequencies, and saying a repeater's call sign does not announce you.
T2A10: A band plan is a voluntary agreement among hams about which parts of a band are used for which modes or activities. It goes beyond the FCC's legal rules, but following it helps everyone share the band politely.
T2A11: Simplex means a station transmits and receives on the same frequency, taking turns talking. Full duplex would use two different frequencies at once, as a repeater does.
T2B01: A repeater listens on its input frequency, which your radio transmits on. The reverse function swaps your radio's transmit and receive frequencies so you can listen there and check whether you can hear other stations directly.
T2B02: CTCSS (continuous tone-coded squelch system) sends a low tone that people cannot hear in the voice audio. A repeater opens its squelch, the receiver's quiet gate, only when it detects the right tone.
T2B03: In a linked repeater network, what one repeater receives is sent out by all of them. That lets a conversation reach a much larger area than one repeater could cover.
T2B04: Hearing a repeater only means its output reaches you. To get in, your radio also needs the right offset, and the right CTCSS tone or DCS (digital coded squelch) code if the repeater requires one. Any of those being wrong could lock you out, so all are correct.
T2B05: If you talk too loudly, your voice peaks push the FM signal wider than the system allows, and the audio can cut out on the loudest parts. Speaking at a normal level and a bit back from the microphone helps.
T2B06: DTMF (dual-tone multi-frequency) is the touch-tone signal, where each key press sends two audio tones at once. Repeaters can use these tones for control functions.
T2B07: A talkgroup on a digital repeater is selected by a group ID number or code, so you program that code into your radio. A registration or special tone is not what puts you in the talkgroup.
T2B08: If two stations interfere on the same frequency, no one owns it just because they were there first. The polite and sensible fix is for the two operators to talk it over and agree how to share or who should move.
T2B09: Simplex channels let hams who are close enough to hear each other talk directly. That keeps repeaters free for people who really need their extra range.
T2B10: QRM means "I am being interfered with" by other stations. A helpful memory hook is that the M can stand for "man-made." QRN, by comparison, means static noise from nature.
T2B11: QSY means "I am changing frequency." Hams often say it when moving a chat to a different frequency to free up a calling channel.
T2B12: On DMR (digital mobile radio), the color code works like a password your radio must have to use a specific repeater. If your radio's color code does not match, the repeater ignores you.
T2B13: Squelch is a gate that silences the speaker when no signal is present, so you do not hear constant hiss. When a signal arrives, the gate opens and you hear the audio.
T2B14: On DMR (digital mobile radio), a talkgroup is an identifier that sorts conversations by group. You only hear the traffic of groups you choose, and other chatter does not bother you.
T2C01: FCC rules say Part 97, the amateur radio rules, always apply whenever you operate an amateur station, even during RACES, ARES, or other emergency activities. Being part of those groups does not give you a pass.
T2C02: A net is an on-air group meeting, and the Net Control Station is like its teacher or host. It opens the net and directs who speaks and when. Choosing the schedule is usually done by the net's organizers, and licensing is each operator's own job.
T2C03: Spelling an unusual word with a standard phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, and so on) makes each letter clear even in noisy conditions. Sending the word in Morse code or asking for it to be repeated back is not the standard technique for this.
T2C04: RACES, the Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service, is part of the FCC's amateur rules. It gives hams a way to help with civil defense communications during national emergencies. It does not involve citizens band radio.
T2C05: In net operation, traffic means the formal messages that stations pass along. It is like mail being carried by radio.
T2C06: ARES, the Amateur Radio Emergency Service, is made up of licensed hams who volunteer and register their skills and equipment to help with communications in public service and emergencies.
T2C07: In a net, you transmit only when the net control station tells you to, unless you have an emergency to report. That keeps things orderly, like raising your hand in class. The other practices listed are not standard requirements.
T2C08: Winlink is a system that sends email over amateur radio, using email addresses based on call signs. FT8, PSK31, and AMTOR are digital modes, not email systems.
T2C09: A control operator may go outside their license privileges only when human life or property is in immediate danger. Emergency plans from FEMA or RACES do not by themselves allow it.
T2C10: The preamble is the front part of a formal traffic message. It holds the information needed to keep track of the message as it is passed along, like the label on a package.
T2C11: In a radiogram header, the check is the count of words, or word equivalents, in the message text. The receiving station counts too, to make sure nothing was lost.
T2C12: RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service) requires certification by a civil defense agency, meaning a government emergency management office. ARES, MARS, and SKYWARN do not require that certification.
T3A01: Radio waves can bounce off buildings and ground and reach your antenna by several paths. Those copies can cancel each other or add together, so moving your antenna just a few feet can change the signal a lot. This is called multipath.
T3A02: Plants and leaves soak up UHF and microwave signals, so weak signals get weaker. That is why a signal may get worse when trees grow or leaf out.
T3A03: Horizontal polarization, meaning the signal's electric field lies sideways, is the usual choice for long-distance CW (Morse code) and SSB (single sideband voice) on VHF and UHF. It is the common standard, so stations match.
T3A04: Cross-polarization means one antenna is vertical and the other horizontal. They do not line up well, like trying to push a sideways slat through a vertical gap, so the received signal gets weaker.
T3A05: If buildings block the straight path, a directional antenna can be aimed at something that bounces the signal toward the repeater, such as a hill or a large building. Signals can reflect, much like light off a mirror.
T3A06: Picket fencing is the rapid fluttering you hear on a moving vehicle's signal. It happens because multipath, the signal arriving by several paths, constantly changes as the vehicle moves.
T3A07: At microwave frequencies, rain, snow, and other precipitation absorb and scatter the signal, which can shorten the range. Wind, pressure, and cold have little effect.
T3A08: Signals bounced by the ionosphere may take several different paths to reach you. When they randomly add and cancel each other, the signal rises and falls irregularly, which is called fading.
T3A09: Ionospheric signals are elliptically polarized, a twisted mix of vertical and horizontal. Because of that, either a vertical or a horizontal antenna can send or receive them well.
T3A10: With multipath, copies of the signal arrive at slightly different times and get mixed up, which scrambles digital data. That makes errors in the received data more likely.
T3A11: The ionosphere is a layer of the upper atmosphere filled with charged particles. It can bend or reflect HF (high frequency) radio waves back toward Earth, like a mirror in the sky.
T3A12: At 10 and 6 meters the waves are long, so fog and rain barely affect them. Rain matters much more at microwave frequencies.
T3B01: The electric and magnetic fields in a radio wave are at right angles to each other, and both are at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
T3B02: A radio wave's polarization is defined by the orientation of its electric field. A vertical antenna makes a vertically polarized wave, and a horizontal antenna makes a horizontally polarized one.
T3B03: A radio wave is made of an electric field and a magnetic field that travel together, each helping to create the other. Voltage and current are in wires, not the wave itself.
T3B04: Radio waves travel through free space at the speed of light. They are far faster than sound, which needs air to travel and moves much more slowly.
T3B05: As frequency goes up, wavelength gets shorter. Picture waves in water: if more waves pass by each second, each one must be shorter.
T3B06: Divide 300 by the frequency in megahertz (MHz) to get the approximate wavelength in meters. For example, 146 MHz gives 300 / 146, which is about 2 meters, which is why that band is called 2 meters.
T3B07: Besides frequency, hams commonly name a band by its approximate wavelength, such as the 2-meter or 70-centimeter band. Channel numbers are not used to name amateur bands, so "all correct" does not fit.
T3B08: VHF, very high frequency, covers 30 MHz to 300 MHz. The popular 2-meter band at about 146 MHz falls in this range.
T3B09: UHF, ultra high frequency, covers 300 to 3000 MHz. The 70-centimeter band at about 440 MHz falls in this range.
T3B10: HF, high frequency, covers 3 to 30 MHz. These are the shortwave bands hams use for long-distance talking around the world.
T3B11: Radio waves travel at about 300,000,000 meters per second in free space, the speed of light. That is also the 300 used in the wavelength formula.
T3B12: All radio waves, whether microwaves, UHF, or VHF, travel at the same speed in free space, the speed of light. Frequency changes the wavelength, not the speed.
T3C01: UHF signals usually are not bent back by the ionosphere, so they travel in nearly straight lines and fade out past the radio horizon. That is why simplex UHF contacts are mostly local.
T3C02: HF signals often bounce off the ionosphere and travel thousands of miles, which is far more common on HF than on VHF or higher. HF antennas are usually bigger, not smaller.
T3C03: Signals bounced off the aurora (the northern lights) sound distorted and raspy, because the moving aurora scrambles them. That unusual sound is the clue to this kind of propagation.
T3C04: Sporadic E happens when small patches of the ionosphere's E layer reflect signals unusually well. It can suddenly bring strong, distant signals on 10, 6, and 2 meters.
T3C05: Knife-edge diffraction is when a radio wave bends slightly around the sharp edge of an obstacle such as a mountain ridge. It lets some signal get past things that block the direct path.
T3C06: Tropospheric ducting happens when a layer of air traps signals and carries them far past the horizon, often about 300 miles, on VHF and UHF. It happens regularly in some areas.
T3C07: The 6-meter band is best for meteor scatter, where signals bounce off the glowing trails of meteors burning up. Those trails reflect lower VHF frequencies best.
T3C08: Tropospheric ducting is caused by temperature inversions, where a layer of warm air sits above cooler air. This traps radio waves in a channel so they travel far.
T3C09: The 10-meter band works best by F region (a high layer of the ionosphere) when sunspot activity is high, and in the daytime from dawn until a little after sunset. The sun's energy charges the ionosphere that reflects the signals.
T3C10: During the peak of the sunspot cycle, the ionosphere can reflect the higher HF and low VHF frequencies, so 6 and 10 meters can carry signals very far. The higher bands, like 70 centimeters and 23 centimeters, go through the ionosphere.
T3C11: The atmosphere bends radio waves slightly downward as they travel, which lets them reach a bit past the visual horizon. This slight bending is called refraction.
T4A01: A mobile radio runs on about 13.8 volts, the normal voltage of a car's electrical system. A 50-watt radio can pull around 10 amperes (amps, the amount of current) while transmitting, so the supply needs to handle 12 amperes. 4 amperes would be too small.
T4A02: An SWR meter (standing wave ratio meter, which shows how well your antenna matches the cable) is built to work over certain frequencies and power levels. Pick one made for the band and power you will actually use, or its readings will be off.
T4A03: Thin or long wires act like a skinny, long hose that resists current, so some voltage gets lost along the way. Short, thick wires lose very little, which keeps the radio's voltage steady when it is transmitting and drawing the most current.
T4A04: FT8 is a digital mode where a computer makes and decodes the signals. The radio's audio output goes into the computer's audio input, and the computer's audio output goes into the radio's audio input. No special terminal unit or website is needed.
T4A05: An RF power meter measures the radio-frequency power going out to the antenna, so it goes in the feed line (the cable) between the transmitter and the antenna. The power supply cable only carries DC power, not the signal you want to measure.
T4A06: A computer and radio need to share three things: sound from the radio to the computer (receive audio), sound from the computer to the radio (transmit audio), and a signal to switch the radio into transmit (keying). Antenna and RF power are not part of that interface.
T4A07: The computer needs to hear what the radio receives, so the computer's "line in" (its audio input) connects to the radio's speaker or audio output. The computer's "line out" goes to the radio's microphone or audio input, not to its speaker connection.
T4A08: At radio frequencies, current travels on the surface of a conductor, so a wide, flat copper strap gives a low-resistance path for bonding (joining metal parts together). Thin wire or braid is not as good, and flat strap is the preferred choice.
T4A09: A battery's ampere-hour rating says how many amps it can supply for one hour. Dividing it by the average current your gear draws gives the hours it will run. For example, a 100 amp-hour battery and a 5 amp load lasts about 20 hours.
T4A10: A digital mode hotspot is a small device that links nearby handheld or mobile radios to a digital voice or data network through the internet. Think of it as a mini gateway that connects your radio to a bigger network.
T4A11: The battery's negative terminal (or the chassis ground point right at the battery) is the most direct, low-resistance return path for the radio's heavy current. Other metal parts of the car may have poor or rusty connections, which can cause voltage drops and noise.
T4A12: An electronic keyer is a device that helps you send Morse code by hand. It makes the dots and dashes with steady timing when you press a paddle, so your sending sounds neat.
T4B01: Too much microphone gain (volume) overloads the transmitter, so your voice sounds distorted and can spill over onto nearby frequencies. Turning the gain down gives clear audio.
T4B02: You can type a frequency on the keypad or turn the VFO (variable frequency oscillator, the main tuning knob). CTCSS and DTMF are tone systems, not frequency entry, and automatic frequency control only fine-tunes a signal, so those are wrong.
T4B03: Squelch is a gate that mutes the speaker when no signal is present. To hear a weak signal, set the threshold so the audio just stays on all the time, so even weak signals can pass. Then you can hear them.
T4B04: An FM receiver is designed to hear a signal right on its frequency. If you are slightly off, the voice sounds distorted or garbled. It does not just get quieter or change pitch.
T4B05: Scanning makes your radio automatically step through a range of frequencies or memory channels. It stops when it finds activity so you can listen in. It is not an antenna test.
T4B06: On a single-sideband (SSB) signal, being slightly off frequency makes a voice sound too high or too low, like a Donald Duck voice. The RIT (receiver incremental tuning), also called the Clarifier, lets you fine-tune the receive frequency to fix it.
T4B07: A code plug is the file of settings you load into a DMR (digital mobile radio) radio. It holds the repeater frequencies, talkgroups, and other options so the radio knows what to use. It is not a cable or a physical plug.
T4B08: A narrower filter lets in less noise and fewer neighboring signals. Choosing a filter width that matches the mode, such as narrow for Morse code and wider for voice, cuts interference and makes signals easier to hear.
T4B09: On DMR, you pick a group by entering its identification code, called a talkgroup ID. Talkgroups are like chat rooms. A CTCSS tone or a different frequency does not select them.
T4B10: An SSB voice signal takes up about 2400 Hz (hertz, cycles per second). A filter that width lets the whole voice through and blocks extra noise. A narrower filter cuts off parts of the voice, and a wider one lets in more noise.
T4B11: A D-STAR radio must have your call sign programmed in before you transmit. D-STAR sends it along with your signal so others know who is talking. The other items are not required to be entered in this way.
T5A01: Electrical current is measured in amperes, often called amps. Think of it as how much water flows through a hose each second. Volts measure push, watts measure power, and ohms measure resistance.
T5A02: Electrical power is measured in watts. Volts measure the electrical push, amperes measure the flow, and watt-hours measure energy used over time, not power.
T5A03: The flow of electrons through a circuit is called current, like water flowing through a hose. Voltage is the push that makes them flow, not the flow itself.
T5A04: Frequency is how many complete cycles an alternating current makes each second. Wavelength is the distance one cycle covers, not how often it repeats.
T5A05: A difference in voltage (electrical pressure) makes electrons flow, just as a difference in water pressure makes water move through a pipe. Without a voltage difference, nothing flows.
T5A06: The unit of frequency is the hertz (Hz), which means one cycle per second. A henry measures inductance and a farad measures capacitance.
T5A07: Metals have many free electrons that can move easily from atom to atom, so they carry current well. Protons stay put inside the atoms and do not flow.
T5A08: Glass holds its electrons tightly and does not let current flow, so it is an insulator. Sea water, stainless steel, and graphite all conduct electricity.
T5A09: Alternating current (AC) flows one way, then reverses and flows the other way, over and over. It swings between positive and negative directions, not just between one direction and zero.
T5A10: Power is how fast electrical energy is used. A 100-watt light bulb uses energy faster than a 10-watt bulb. Resistance, current, and voltage describe other things.
T5A11: Resistance opposes every kind of current, whether it is direct current (DC, flowing one way), alternating current (AC), or RF (radio frequency) current. All of the statements are true.
T5B01: Milli means one thousandth, so one ampere is 1000 milliamperes. Multiply: 1.5 amperes x 1000 = 1500 milliamperes.
T5B02: Kilo means 1000, so divide the hertz by 1000 to get kilohertz (kHz). 1,500,000 hertz / 1000 = 1500 kHz.
T5B03: The prefix kilo means one thousand. So one kilovolt is 1000 volts.
T5B04: The prefix micro means one-millionth. So one microvolt is one one-millionth of a volt.
T5B05: Milli means one thousandth, so 1000 milliwatts make one watt. 500 milliwatts / 1000 = 0.5 watts, or half a watt.
T5B06: Milli means one thousandth, so divide milliamperes by 1000 to get amperes. 3000 / 1000 = 3 amperes.
T5B07: One MHz (megahertz) is 1000 kHz (kilohertz). Multiply: 3.525 x 1000 = 3525 kHz.
T5B08: Pico means one-trillionth and micro means one-millionth, so 1,000,000 picofarads make one microfarad. A farad is the unit of capacitance, the ability to store electric charge.
T5B09: Doubling power is an increase of about 3 dB (decibels, a way to compare power levels). Going from 5 watts to 10 watts is a doubling, so it is about 3 dB.
T5B10: Each halving of power is about -3 dB (decibels, a way to compare power levels). Going from 12 watts to 6 watts to 3 watts is two halvings, so -3 dB + -3 dB = -6 dB.
T5B11: A decibel (dB) compares power levels. Every ten-times increase in power adds 10 dB. Going from 20 watts to 200 watts is ten times more, so it is 10 dB.
T5B12: Mega means a million and kilo means a thousand, so 1 MHz is 1000 kHz. Divide: 28,400 kHz / 1000 = 28.400 MHz.
T5B13: One GHz (gigahertz) is 1000 MHz (megahertz). Divide: 2425 MHz / 1000 = 2.425 GHz.
T5C01: Capacitance is the ability to store energy in an electric field, like a tiny rechargeable bucket of charge. Inductance stores energy in a magnetic field instead.
T5C02: The unit of capacitance is the farad. The ohm measures resistance, the volt measures electrical push, and the henry measures inductance.
T5C03: Inductance is the ability to store energy in a magnetic field, as a coil of wire does. Capacitance stores energy in an electric field instead.
T5C04: The unit of inductance is the henry. A farad measures capacitance, an ohm measures resistance, and a coulomb measures electric charge.
T5C05: Impedance is measured in ohms, the same unit as resistance. Impedance is how much a circuit opposes alternating current.
T5C06: Kilo is written with a lowercase k, and hertz is written with a capital H, so kilohertz is kHz. The capital letter in Hz honors a scientist named Hertz.
T5C07: Mega is written with a capital M, since lowercase m means milli (one thousandth). Hertz is Hz with a capital H, so megahertz is MHz.
T5C08: Power in watts equals current in amperes times voltage in volts. In letters, that is P = I x E. More current or more voltage means more power.
T5C09: Power equals voltage times current. 13.8 volts x 10 amperes = 138 watts.
T5C10: Power equals voltage times current. 12 volts x 2.5 amperes = 30 watts.
T5C11: Power equals voltage times current, so current equals power divided by voltage. 120 watts / 12 volts = 10 amperes.
T5C12: Impedance is the total opposition a circuit gives to alternating current (AC). It combines plain resistance with the extra opposition from capacitors and coils. It is measured in ohms.
T5D01: This is Ohm's Law, where current (I) equals voltage (E) divided by resistance (R). More resistance means less current for the same voltage, like a narrower hose letting less water through.
T5D02: This is Ohm's Law. Voltage (E) equals current (I) times resistance (R). The more current pushed through a resistor, the more voltage it takes.
T5D03: This is Ohm's Law. Resistance (R) equals voltage (E) divided by current (I). It tells how many volts it takes to push one ampere through.
T5D04: Resistance equals voltage divided by current. 90 volts / 3 amperes = 30 ohms.
T5D05: Resistance equals voltage divided by current. 12 volts / 1.5 amperes = 8 ohms.
T5D06: Resistance equals voltage divided by current. 12 volts / 4 amperes = 3 ohms.
T5D07: Current equals voltage divided by resistance. 120 volts / 80 ohms = 1.5 amperes.
T5D08: Current equals voltage divided by resistance. 200 volts / 100 ohms = 2 amperes.
T5D09: Current equals voltage divided by resistance. 240 volts / 24 ohms = 10 amperes.
T5D10: Voltage equals current times resistance. 0.5 amperes x 2 ohms = 1 volt.
T5D11: Voltage equals current times resistance. 1 ampere x 10 ohms = 10 volts.
T5D12: Voltage equals current times resistance. 2 amperes x 10 ohms = 20 volts.
T5D13: In a series circuit, the parts are connected in a single loop, so all the current has just one path. Like cars on a one-lane road, the same number pass every point.
T5D14: In a parallel circuit, every part connects across the same two points, so each one gets the same voltage. Like several taps on one water pipe, each gets the same pressure.
T6A01: A resistor opposes, or resists, the flow of current, a bit like a narrow spot in a hose slows the water. Inductors and transformers mostly react to changing current, and an inverter changes DC into AC.
T6A02: A potentiometer is a resistor you can adjust by turning a knob, so it works as a volume control. A fixed resistor has one set value and cannot be adjusted.
T6A03: A potentiometer controls resistance, which is how much the part opposes current. Turning the knob changes how much resistance is in the circuit.
T6A04: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field, like a tiny rechargeable bucket of charge. An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field instead.
T6A05: A capacitor is built from two conductive plates (surfaces) with an insulator between them. That gap is what lets it store energy in an electric field.
T6A06: An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field when current flows through it. A capacitor stores energy in an electric field instead.
T6A07: An inductor is usually a coil of wire, and the coil shape is what builds up the magnetic field. Capacitors, diodes, and transistors are not made as wire coils.
T6A08: SPDT means single-pole, double-throw. One circuit is switched between two other circuits, like a railroad switch sending a train down one of two tracks.
T6A09: Component 3 in figure T-2 is a switch drawn as a simple gap with one moving blade, so it opens or closes one circuit. That is a single-pole, single-throw (SPST) switch, just an on-off switch.
T6A10: Nickel-metal hydride, lithium-ion, and lead-acid batteries can all be recharged many times. Since each statement is true, all of these choices are correct.
T6A11: Carbon-zinc batteries are the common cheap throwaway type and should not be recharged. Nickel-cadmium, lead-acid, and lithium-ion batteries are all made to be recharged.
T6B01: Forward voltage drop is the small voltage lost across a diode when it conducts, and it differs by diode type. For example, Schottky diodes lose less than ordinary silicon diodes, and a drop is normal, not a sign of damage.
T6B02: A diode works like a one-way valve for electricity, letting current flow in only one direction. A resistor and a fuse do not care which way current flows.
T6B03: A transistor can turn current on and off using a small control signal, so it works as an electronic switch. A varistor, potentiometer, and thermistor change resistance, but they are not normally used as on-off switches.
T6B04: A bipolar transistor is built from three layers (regions) of semiconductor material, such as NPN or PNP. Triodes and pentodes are vacuum tubes, and an alternator is a generator.
T6B05: A field-effect transistor (FET) has a gate, drain, and source. A bipolar junction transistor uses emitter, base, and collector instead.
T6B06: Diodes often have a stripe or band painted near the cathode end. That stripe is a quick way to tell which way the diode is facing.
T6B07: An LED, a light-emitting diode, glows when current flows through it in the forward direction. Reverse current is blocked, so it makes no light.
T6B08: FET stands for Field Effect Transistor. The name comes from the way an electric field at the gate controls the current.
T6B09: The two electrodes of a diode are the anode and the cathode. Current flows in at the anode and out at the cathode. Source, drain, gate, and base belong to transistors.
T6B10: A transistor can give power gain, meaning more power comes out than goes in, because a small signal controls a larger current. Transformers, reactors, and resistors cannot make a signal stronger in power.
T6B11: Gain compares output to input, and it can be measured as voltage, current, or power. All three statements describe gain, so all of these choices are correct.
T6B12: A bipolar junction transistor has three leads called the emitter, base, and collector. The other word sets are not real transistor part names.
T6C01: A schematic is a diagram that uses standard symbols to show what parts a circuit has and how they connect. Think of it as a map of the circuit.
T6C02: Component 1 in figure T-1 is drawn as a zigzag line, which is the symbol for a resistor. The zigzag stands for the part resisting current.
T6C03: Component 2 in figure T-1 is a circle with a vertical bar and a pair of angled leads, one with an arrow. That is the symbol for a transistor.
T6C04: Component 3 in figure T-1 is a small rounded bulb symbol, which is a lamp. It lights when current flows through it.
T6C05: Component 4 in figure T-1 is a stack of long and short parallel lines, which is the symbol for a battery. Ground is the three slanted lines, shown separately.
T6C06: Component 6 in figure T-2 is drawn as two close, parallel plates with a gap, which is the symbol for a capacitor. It looks like the part itself, two plates and an insulator.
T6C07: Component 8 in figure T-2 is a diode symbol with small arrows pointing away from it. Those arrows mean it gives off light, so it is a light emitting diode (LED).
T6C08: Component 9 in figure T-2 is a zigzag resistor symbol with an arrow through or against it. The arrow means the value can be adjusted, so it is a variable resistor.
T6C09: Component 4 in figure T-2 is two coils of wire facing each other with parallel lines between them. That is the symbol for a transformer.
T6C10: Component 3 in figure T-3 is a coil with an arrow touching it, so you can slide to different points on the coil. A coil is an inductor, and the arrow makes it variable.
T6C11: Component 4 in figure T-3 is a symbol shaped like an upside-down triangle on a stem, the standard symbol for an antenna.
T6C12: A schematic shows how parts are connected, not how they look or how long the wires are. So component connections are what it shows accurately.
T6D01: A rectifier changes alternating current (AC), which flows back and forth, into direct current (DC) that flows one way. Diodes are often used to build rectifiers.
T6D02: A relay is a switch operated by electricity. A small current in a coil makes a magnet that closes or opens the switch contacts, so a small signal can control a bigger circuit.
T6D03: Shielded wire has a metal covering that blocks stray signals from getting in or out of the wire. That prevents unwanted coupling of signals, which helps with noise and interference.
T6D04: A meter shows an electrical quantity, like volts or amps, as a number or a needle reading. A potentiometer, transistor, and relay do other jobs.
T6D05: A regulator circuit keeps the output voltage of a power supply steady at the right level. An oscillator makes a signal and a filter smooths out ripple.
T6D06: A transformer changes AC voltage from one level to another, such as stepping 120 volts down to a lower voltage. Diodes and transistors do not do that, and a variable capacitor only adjusts capacitance.
T6D07: An LED lights up when current flows through it, so it is commonly used as an indicator light. A FET and a Zener diode are not used to make light.
T6D08: A capacitor combined with an inductor makes a resonant circuit, which responds strongly at one particular frequency. The two parts trade energy back and forth, like a swing.
T6D09: An integrated circuit, or IC, packs many semiconductors and other parts into one small package. It is often called a chip.
T6D10: Component 2 in figure T-1 is a transistor. A small signal fed to one of its leads (the base) controls a larger current flowing through it, so it controls the flow of current. The lamp is what gives off light, and the battery supplies the energy.
T6D11: A resonant, or tuned, circuit is an inductor and a capacitor connected together in series or in parallel. The pair is tuned to respond to one frequency, which is how radios pick a station.
T0A01: A 12-volt battery can deliver a huge current if its terminals are shorted by a wrench or wire. That can cause burns, fire, or an explosion. 12 volts is very unlikely to shock you through your hands, and RF does not make the battery release gas.
T0A02: Current through the body can heat tissue, disrupt the electrical signals of cells, and make muscles contract involuntarily. All three are real hazards, so all of these choices are correct.
T0A03: In US 120 V AC wiring, black insulation marks the hot wire, which carries the voltage. White is neutral and green or bare is equipment ground.
T0A04: A fuse is a deliberate weak link that melts and removes power if too much current flows (an overload). It does not smooth ripple or protect you from shocks.
T0A05: A 20-ampere fuse would let far more current flow before it blew, so wires could overheat and start a fire. The fuse size is chosen to protect the wiring and equipment. A bigger fuse is not safer.
T0A06: Three-wire cords, a common safety ground, and fully discharged high-voltage capacitors each reduce shock risk. All three tips are good, so all of these choices are correct.
T0A07: A lightning arrester belongs on a grounded panel near where the feed lines enter the building. That way a surge is sent to ground outside before it reaches your radio.
T0A08: A fuse or circuit breaker goes in series with the hot conductor only, so it can cut off the voltage-carrying wire. Series means the current has to pass through it, like a gate on a single road.
T0A09: Ground rods and earth connections should be bonded together with heavy wire or strap. That keeps them at the same voltage, so no dangerous voltage can appear between them.
T0A10: Charging or discharging a battery too quickly makes it hot and can make it release gas, which is called out-gassing. That can cause damage, fire, or even an explosion.
T0A11: Filter capacitors in a power supply can stay charged after it is switched off, and that stored charge can shock you. Always discharge them before working inside.
T0A12: A voltmeter and its leads must be rated for the voltage you are measuring, or insulation could fail and shock you. A good voltmeter has high impedance (a high resistance to current), not low, and the circuit does not need to be grounded through it.
T0B01: Lightning ground connections should be short and direct. Lightning current moves fast and does not like long paths or sharp turns, and a drip loop or right-angle bends would make things worse.
T0B02: Climbing a tower safely takes training, tying off to the tower at all times, and wearing an approved climbing harness. All three are required, so all of these choices are correct.
T0B03: Never climb a tower without a helper or observer. If something goes wrong up high, you need someone below who can call for help, no matter how high or what kind of work.
T0B04: When putting up a tower, look for overhead power lines and stay well clear of them. Contact with high-voltage lines can be deadly. A wrist ground strap and an insulated base would not protect you.
T0B05: A safety wire through a turnbuckle keeps it from slowly loosening because of vibration. That helps the guy line stay tight and the tower stay steady.
T0B06: Keep enough distance that if the antenna fell, no part could come within 10 feet of the power wires. Plan for the worst case so a fall cannot cause contact.
T0B07: A crank-up tower should not be climbed unless it is retracted or mechanical safety locks are in place. Otherwise it could suddenly drop. Crank-up towers should be grounded and may be painted.
T0B08: A good tower ground uses separate eight-foot ground rods for each leg, bonded to the tower and to each other. A single short rod, a choke, or a water pipe alone would not safely carry lightning current.
T0B09: A utility pole carries high-voltage power lines, and an antenna attached to it could touch them. That could be deadly, which is the main reason to stay away.
T0B10: Lightning is fast and does not like sharp corners, so ground conductors should avoid sharp bends and use gentle curves. Insulated wire is fine and common grounds are actually wanted.
T0B11: Grounding rules for towers and antennas come from local electrical codes. The FCC Part 97 rules do not set those electrical grounding requirements.
T0C01: Radio signals are non-ionizing radiation. They do not have enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, unlike gamma or alpha radiation.
T0C02: The lowest maximum permissible exposure (MPE) is in the 30 to 300 MHz range, because the body absorbs RF most easily there. Of these choices, 50 MHz is in that range.
T0C03: At 50 percent duty cycle, the transmitter is on only half the time, so the average exposure is half. The allowable power density therefore goes up by a factor of 2 (1 divided by 0.5 equals 2).
T0C04: RF exposure depends on frequency, power, distance from the antenna, and the antenna's radiation pattern. All of those matter, so all of these choices are correct.
T0C05: The human body absorbs RF energy better at some frequencies than at others, so the safe limits change with frequency. Lower frequency does not mean more energy.
T0C06: You can check compliance by calculation from the OET Bulletin 65 guidelines, by computer modeling, or by measuring with calibrated equipment. All are acceptable, so all of these choices are correct.
T0C07: Touching an antenna while transmitting can cause an RF burn to your skin. The RF is not ionizing radiation, and an RF burn is a heating injury.
T0C08: Moving the antennas farther from where people are can reduce exposure. Raising the duty cycle would increase exposure, and relocating the transmitter alone does not change where the energy is radiated.
T0C09: Re-evaluate your station whenever you change something in the transmitter or antenna system, because power, gain, or pattern may change your exposure. Low SWR does not guarantee compliance.
T0C10: Duty cycle affects the average exposure, because RF safety limits are based on exposure averaged over time. A transmitter that is on less of the time delivers less average energy.
T0C11: Duty cycle is the percentage of time a transmitter is actually transmitting during the averaging time. If it sends half the time, the duty cycle is 50 percent.
T0C12: RF radiation does not have enough energy to cause chemical changes in cells or damage DNA, unlike ionizing radiation. That does not mean it is perfectly safe at high levels, since heating can still harm.
T0C13: The station licensee, which is you if it is your license, is responsible for making sure no one is exposed above the FCC limits. Neighbors and the FCC do not take on that job.
T7A01: Sensitivity is how well a receiver can pick up faint signals. A very sensitive receiver can hear a whisper-quiet station. Selectivity is different: it is about telling signals apart.
T7A02: A transceiver is a radio that combines a transmitter (sends signals) and a receiver (hears signals) in one box. The name is just "transmitter" and "receiver" squeezed together.
T7A03: A mixer combines signals so the result includes a new frequency, which is how radios shift a signal from one frequency to another. An amplifier only makes a signal bigger and does not change its frequency.
T7A04: Selectivity is a receiver's ability to pick one signal out of a crowd of nearby signals. Think of listening to one friend at a noisy party. Sensitivity is different, because it is about hearing weak signals.
T7A05: An oscillator is a circuit that makes a steady signal at a chosen frequency, a bit like a swing that keeps going back and forth at a steady pace. Filters only block or pass signals; they do not create them.
T7A06: A transverter takes a radio's transmit and receive signals and shifts them to a different band. For example, it lets a radio built for one band work on another. Filters only block certain frequencies and do not move them.
T7A07: PTT stands for Push-To-Talk. When the PTT input is grounded, which is what pressing the mic button does, the radio switches from receive to transmit. It is like a switch between listening and talking.
T7A08: Modulation means combining your voice (or other information) with an RF carrier signal, which is the radio wave that carries it through the air. Oscillation only makes a steady signal and does not add speech to it.
T7A09: Different modes, like SSB (single sideband voice) and CW-FM (Morse code or FM), need the amplifier to work a little differently. The switch sets the amplifier for the mode you are using. It does not change the signal your radio sends.
T7A10: An RF power amplifier, sometimes called a linear amplifier, boosts a transceiver's output to a higher power. A potentiometer is just a variable resistor, and "impedance multiplier" is not a power booster.
T7A11: The VFO, or Variable Frequency Oscillator, is the circuit behind the tuning knob. It sets the frequency the radio receives and transmits on, so turning the dial changes the VFO.
T7B01: Over-deviation means an FM signal is swinging too wide, often because audio is too strong. Talking farther from the microphone makes the audio weaker and fixes it. Talking louder would make it worse.
T7B02: Broadcast AM and FM radios can be overloaded by strong nearby signals from outside their own band, because they cannot reject them well enough. The problem is in the receiver, not in how you talk or set your microphone.
T7B03: Radio frequency interference can come from fundamental overload (a very strong signal swamping a receiver), harmonics (extra signals at multiples of your frequency), and spurious emissions (unwanted signals your transmitter sends). All three are true causes.
T7B04: A high SWR (standing wave ratio, which means power is bouncing back because the antenna is mismatched) makes many solid-state transmitters turn their power down to protect themselves. So low output can point to high SWR. A low SWR is a good thing.
T7B05: A filter at the receiver's antenna input stops your signal before it reaches the receiver's circuits, which is where overloading happens. A filter on your own transmitter only helps when the interference is unwanted extra signals from your transmitter, not overload.
T7B06: First, check that your own station works properly and does not interfere with your own radio or TV tuned to the same channel. That is a calm first step. Shutting down and calling the FCC right away is not needed yet.
T7B07: A band-reject filter blocks the range of frequencies where the strong commercial FM station is, so it cannot overload your 2-meter radio. A preamplifier would boost the unwanted signal too.
T7B08: All of these are good steps. Work with your neighbor to find the device that is making noise, politely explain that FCC rules cover devices causing interference, and make sure your own station follows good amateur practice.
T7B09: Loose or poorly installed coaxial connectors are a common cause of cable TV interference, and they are the easiest thing to check, so start there. Filters may help later if the problem remains.
T7B10: All of these can distort your voice on a repeater. Being slightly off frequency, speaking too loudly or too close to the microphone, or being in a poor location can each make your audio sound bad.
T7B11: RF from your own transmitter can sneak back into the microphone cable and distort your voice. A ferrite choke is a small clip-on block that stops that RF from flowing along the cable.
T7C01: A dummy load is a safe stand-in for an antenna that soaks up your transmitter's power as heat. It lets you test your radio without sending signals out over the air.
T7C02: An antenna analyzer checks an antenna across frequencies and shows where it is resonant, meaning where it works best. The other instruments listed do not directly test antenna resonance.
T7C03: A dummy load is basically a 50-ohm resistor that does not add inductance, mounted on a heat sink. The heat sink carries away the heat made when it absorbs your transmitter's power.
T7C04: SWR, the standing wave ratio, measures how well the antenna matches the feed line. A perfect match is 1:1, which means no power is reflected back. Higher numbers mean a worse match.
T7C05: High SWR means power reflects back toward the transmitter, which can damage its output transistors. Many solid-state radios lower their power automatically to protect those parts.
T7C06: An SWR of 4:1 is quite high, which means the antenna and feed line are not well matched, so some power is reflected back. A perfect match would be 1:1. It is not a gain or loss in dB.
T7C07: Power lost in a feed line, the cable between your radio and antenna, turns into heat. It does not become radio waves or reach the antenna. That is why long, poor cables waste power.
T7C08: A directional wattmeter measures forward power and reflected power, and from those you can work out the SWR. A voltmeter or ohmmeter cannot do that.
T7C09: Water getting into coax is a leading cause of failure, because it raises loss and corrodes the cable. Good weather sealing helps keep it out.
T7C10: Ultraviolet light from the sun can crack and weaken the outer jacket, which lets water seep into the cable and ruin it. So the jacket should resist UV.
T7C11: Foam-dielectric coax has less loss per foot than solid-dielectric coax. The dielectric is the insulating material between the inner wire and the shield. Foam cable usually handles moisture worse, not better.
T7D01: Electric potential is another name for voltage, and a voltmeter measures it. An ammeter measures current, and an ohmmeter measures resistance.
T7D02: A voltmeter connects in parallel, meaning across the two ends of the component, like putting a pressure gauge across a hose. Connecting it in series would break up the circuit.
T7D03: To measure current, the meter must be in series, so the current flows through the meter, like counting cars passing one spot on a single road. The circuit has to be opened to put the meter in line.
T7D04: An ammeter measures electric current, which is how much electricity is flowing, measured in amps. A voltmeter measures voltage and an ohmmeter measures resistance.
T7D05: An ohmmeter sends a small known current through the part and measures the resulting voltage. From that it calculates the resistance using Ohm's law.
T7D06: A multimeter set to measure resistance supplies its own tiny current, so connecting it to a live voltage can damage it. Always switch to the right setting before probing a live circuit.
T7D07: A multimeter measures voltage and resistance, and usually current too. Things like impedance, reactance, and signal strength need different instruments.
T7D08: Acid-core solder uses acid flux that corrodes electronics, so it is only for plumbing. Rosin-core solder is the right choice for radio and electronics work.
T7D09: A cold solder joint did not melt properly, so it looks rough or lumpy instead of smooth and shiny. These joints can connect poorly, so reheat them.
T7D10: The ohmmeter's small current charges the capacitor, so the voltage rises and the reading shows resistance that keeps increasing over time. Eventually it looks like an open circuit.
T7D11: Turn the circuit's power off before measuring resistance. The ohmmeter supplies its own tiny current, and voltage already in the circuit would give a wrong reading or damage the meter.
T9A01: A beam antenna, like a Yagi, concentrates your signal in one direction. That makes it stronger toward the station you aim at, much like a flashlight beam compared to a bare bulb.
T9A02: Loading adds inductors, which are coils, to make an antenna act electrically longer than it physically is. This lets a shorter antenna resonate on a lower frequency.
T9A03: An antenna's polarization is the direction of its electric field, such as vertical or horizontal. A vertical antenna sends out vertically polarized waves.
T9A04: A short flexible antenna on a handheld, often called a rubber duck, is less efficient than a full quarter-wave antenna, so less of your power is radiated as signal. Efficiency is how much power becomes radio waves.
T9A05: A shorter dipole resonates at a higher frequency, because antenna length and frequency work opposite each other. Lengthening it, adding coils, or adding capacitive loading lowers the frequency.
T9A06: A Yagi concentrates its signal in one direction, so it has the greatest gain here. An isotropic antenna is a theoretical reference that radiates equally in all directions, so it has no gain.
T9A07: The metal body of a car shields radio waves, which weakens the signal going out and coming in. An outside antenna avoids that problem.
T9A08: A quarter-wavelength on 2 meters is about 19 inches, since 2 meters is roughly 79 inches and a quarter of that is about 19.5 inches. So a 19-inch vertical is a resonant quarter-wave antenna.
T9A09: A 5/8-wavelength whip squeezes more signal toward the horizon than a 1/4-wave one, so it has more gain. Gain means stronger signal in a favorable direction.
T9A10: A half-wave dipole radiates strongest broadside, meaning at right angles to the wire, and weakest off its ends. Picture a donut with the wire through the hole.
T9A11: Antenna gain is how much stronger a signal is in a particular direction compared with a reference antenna. The antenna does not add power. It just focuses what it has.
T9B01: PL259, BNC, and Type N connectors are all not fully waterproof, so all of them should be carefully taped or sealed when used outdoors to keep water out.
T9B02: Most amateur radio coax is 50 ohms, which matches the output of most radios and antennas. Ohms measure how much the cable resists the flow of AC signals.
T9B03: Coax is easy to use and does not need many special precautions, such as keeping it away from metal. Other feed lines may have less loss or more power handling, but coax is the simplest.
T9B04: An antenna tuner matches the antenna system's impedance to the radio's output so the radio sees a good load. It does not change the antenna itself. It helps your radio send power to the antenna.
T9B05: As frequency goes up, the loss in coax gets bigger. That is why high-frequency signals need low-loss cable, especially on long runs.
T9B06: Type N connectors work well above 400 MHz and are weather-resistant. PL-259 connectors lose performance at higher frequencies. RS-213 is a cable type, and DB-25 is a computer connector.
T9B07: PL-259 connectors are commonly used at HF and VHF frequencies. They are not watertight and are not suited to microwaves, and they screw on rather than twist like bayonet types.
T9B08: All of these cause loss in coaxial feed line: water getting into connectors, high SWR, and many connectors in the line. Each one wastes some of your signal.
T9B09: A loose connection in the antenna or feed line makes the SWR jump around because the electrical contact keeps changing. Wiggling the cable and tightening connectors can help find it.
T9B10: RG-213 is thicker than RG-58, and it has less loss at a given frequency. RG-58 is thinner and cheaper, but it wastes more of your signal, especially over long runs.
T9B11: Air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss of these feed lines. It is stiff and expensive, but it wastes the least signal.
T9B12: SWR, or standing wave ratio, tells you how well a load, such as an antenna, is matched to its transmission line. A low SWR means a good match, and a high SWR means more power is reflected.
T8A01: Single sideband (SSB) is a form of amplitude modulation, which means the signal's strength carries the voice. SSB just keeps one half of the AM signal and drops the rest. Packet radio and PSK are data methods, not AM.
T8A02: VHF packet radio usually sends its data tones over FM (frequency modulation) or PM (phase modulation), the same kind of signal used by VHF repeaters. SSB and AM are not the usual choice for VHF packet.
T8A03: Single sideband (SSB) is the voice mode favored for weak, long-distance contacts on VHF and UHF. It packs all its power into a narrow slice of spectrum, so faint signals are easier to hear than with FM.
T8A04: VHF and UHF voice repeaters normally use FM (frequency modulation) or PM (phase modulation). It sounds clear and quiet on local contacts, and almost all handheld radios are built for it.
T8A05: CW, or Morse code, is just a tone switched on and off, so it takes up the least room on the dial. SSB voice, FM voice and slow-scan TV (pictures sent as sound) all need much more.
T8A06: Hams use upper sideband (USB) on 10 meters and all the VHF and UHF bands. Lower sideband is the habit on the lower HF bands, like 40 and 80 meters, so USB is the answer for these higher bands.
T8A07: A single sideband (SSB) signal is narrower than FM, only about 3 kHz wide compared with 10 to 15 kHz for FM. Narrower means more signals fit on a band, and the power is focused into less space.
T8A08: A typical single sideband (SSB) voice signal is about 3 kHz wide. That is roughly the range of frequencies needed for understandable speech, like an old telephone.
T8A09: An FM voice signal on a VHF repeater is about 10 to 15 kHz wide. That is much wider than SSB voice, but far narrower than a TV signal.
T8A10: An AM fast-scan TV signal is about 6 MHz wide. Moving pictures carry far more information than voice, so TV needs thousands of times more room than a voice signal.
T8A11: A CW (Morse code) signal needs only about 150 Hz of bandwidth. It is just a simple tone switched on and off, which is why it is the narrowest of the common modes.
T8A12: One drawback of FM is that only one signal can be received at a time. If two stations transmit together, the stronger one captures the receiver and the weaker one disappears, while SSB lets you hear both. FM voice quality is actually good.
T8B01: Satellite beacons send telemetry, which is measurements radioed back from the satellite, such as its health and status. Think of it like a dashboard readout: battery, temperature, and so on. It does not report your signal strength or the exact time.
T8B02: If you use too much effective radiated power (the power your antenna actually sends out) on a satellite uplink, your signal can hog the satellite's receiver. That blocks access for other users who are trying to share it.
T8B03: Satellite tracking programs do all of these things. They show a map of where the satellite is right now, list when each pass starts, peaks and ends along with where to point, and show the Doppler-shifted frequency to tune.
T8B04: Amateur satellites use many modes. Some carry SSB voice, some carry FM voice, and some send CW or data. Each of the choices is something you can find on amateur satellites.
T8B05: A satellite beacon is a transmission from the satellite that contains status information, like a lighthouse that keeps announcing how the satellite is doing. It is not an antenna, a light, or a reflector.
T8B06: A tracking program needs the Keplerian elements, a set of numbers that describe the satellite's orbit. With them it can calculate where the satellite is at any moment. Transmit power and past Doppler timing are not inputs.
T8B07: Doppler shift is a change in the frequency you hear caused by the satellite and you moving toward or away from each other. It is like a passing ambulance siren sounding higher as it comes and lower as it leaves.
T8B08: U/V mode means the uplink (what you send up) is in the UHF band and the downlink (what you hear back) is in the VHF band. In this question that is 70 centimeters up and 2 meters down. The letters stand for UHF and VHF, not ultraviolet.
T8B09: Spin fading happens because the satellite and its antennas are rotating. As the antenna turns, the signal you receive gets stronger and weaker in a repeating pattern, like a spinning flashlight sweeping past you.
T8B10: LEO stands for Low Earth Orbit. These satellites fly close to Earth and circle the planet in roughly 100 minutes, so each pass gives you only a short window of contact.
T8B11: Anyone is allowed to receive telemetry from an amateur satellite. Listening is open to everyone, and amateur satellite signals are not encrypted.
T8B12: A linear transponder is a satellite relay that retransmits many signals at once, so it works best when everyone is about equally strong. Your downlink signal should sound about as strong as the satellite's beacon. If it is much weaker your uplink power is too low, and if it is much stronger you may be crowding out others.
T8C01: Radio direction finding (RDF) uses a directional antenna and a receiver to find which way a signal is coming from. Taking readings from different spots helps you track down a source of noise or jamming.
T8C02: A directional antenna is the tool for a hidden transmitter hunt, because it picks up the signal best when pointed toward the transmitter. An SWR meter or directional wattmeter checks your own transmitter and antenna system, not where a hidden signal is.
T8C03: Contesting means trying to make contact with as many stations as possible within a set time. Nets, hidden transmitter hunts and emergency exercises are different activities with different goals.
T8C04: In a contest, good practice is to send only what is needed: your call sign and the contest exchange. Keeping it short lets more stations get through. Sending partial calls or contacting a station twice only causes confusion.
T8C05: A grid locator is a letter-number code for a geographic location, like 'FN31'. Hams swap them to say roughly where they are on the map. It is not a tool or an antenna direction.
T8C06: You use DTMF (Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency) signals, which are the touch-tone sounds of a keypad, to control an IRLP node over the air. Pressing the right digits tells the node which distant node to connect to.
T8C07: VoIP, or Voice over Internet Protocol, is a way of sending voice conversations over the internet using digital data. It is the same idea behind internet phone calls.
T8C08: The Internet Radio Linking Project (IRLP) connects amateur radio systems, such as repeaters, to each other through the internet. That lets people on different repeaters in different places talk together.
T8C09: EchoLink lets a station transmit through a repeater without using a radio to start it, since you can connect from a computer or smartphone over the internet. IRLP, D-STAR and DMR all normally start from a radio.
T8C10: Before using EchoLink you must register your call sign and give proof that you are licensed. This keeps the system for real amateurs. No training, purchase or General license is required.
T8C11: A gateway is an amateur station that connects other amateur stations to the internet. A repeater only retransmits radio signals, a digipeater relays packet data over radio, and a beacon just sends out a signal.
T8D01: All of these are digital modes. Packet radio sends data in small bundles, IEEE 802.11 is the Wi-Fi standard, and FT8 is a popular weak-signal digital mode.
T8D02: FT8 is a digital mode that can work even when signals are very weak and buried in noise (low signal-to-noise). It sends short, tightly timed messages that a computer can decode when your ears could not.
T8D03: APRS (Automatic Packet Reporting System) can send all of these: GPS position data, short text messages and weather station data. Each one is true.
T8D04: NTSC is the analog fast-scan color TV signal standard used in North America. Hams use it to send moving pictures. It is not an encryption method or a satellite mode.
T8D05: APRS gives real-time tactical digital communications along with a map that shows where stations are. It is how you can watch a vehicle or a weather station move or appear on a map.
T8D06: PSK stands for Phase Shift Keying. The data is sent by shifting the phase, or timing, of a steady signal's wave back and forth.
T8D07: DMR (Digital Mobile Radio) uses time-multiplexing to put two digital voice signals on one 12.5 kHz repeater channel. They take turns in fast time slots, like two people sharing one lane by alternating.
T8D08: Packet radio does all of these. It adds a checksum, which is a number the receiver uses to spot errors. It has a header with the destination call sign. It also uses automatic repeat request (ARQ), asking for a resend if something got damaged.
T8D09: CW stands for continuous wave and is another name for a Morse code transmission. The signal is simply turned on and off to make dots and dashes.
T8D10: The WSJT-X software suite supports all of these. It handles Earth-Moon-Earth (bouncing signals off the Moon), weak signal propagation beacons, and meteor scatter (bouncing signals off meteor trails).
T8D11: ARQ stands for Automatic Repeat reQuest. The receiving station checks for errors and, if it finds any, asks the sender to send that part again, like asking a friend to repeat a sentence you missed.
T8D12: An amateur radio mesh network is a data network built from commercial Wi-Fi equipment loaded with modified firmware. Each node can pass data along to others, forming a web that can keep working even if parts are lost.
